bonding-acidbase.name: Bonding, resonance and acid–base chemistry
bonding-acidbase.description: Check hybrid orbitals, resonance and inductive effects, comparing acid strength with pKa and predicting the direction of acid–base equilibria, with multiple-choice questions. Calculation questions using typical values come with explanations too.
bonding-acidbase.intro:
The shapes and reactivity of organic molecules are set by the hybridization of carbon (sp³, sp², sp) and by where electrons are pulled and how far they spread. The inductive effect, caused by differences in electronegativity, and resonance, in which π electrons and lone pairs are delocalized, are the two pillars for explaining how readily reactions occur.
Acid strength is compared with pKa: as rough values, carboxylic acids are about 4–5, phenol about 10, water 15.7 and alcohols about 16. The more stable the conjugate base, the stronger the acid, and an acid–base equilibrium lies toward the weaker acid, the one with the larger pKa. With this view you can decide how to separate compounds by extraction and which base to use in a reaction.

stereochem.name: Stereochemistry and conformation
stereochem.description: Check chirality, R/S assignment with the CIP priority rules, enantiomers and diastereomers, meso compounds, enantiomeric excess and the chair conformation of cyclohexane with multiple-choice questions.
stereochem.intro:
A molecule that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image is called chiral, and most such molecules contain an asymmetric carbon (chiral center), a carbon bearing four different substituents. Configuration is described as R or S by ranking the substituents with the CIP priority rules, and it is a separate quantity from the direction of optical rotation (+/−). A molecule with n asymmetric carbons has at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers, but fewer when meso compounds exist.
Enantiomers behave identically in an achiral environment, while diastereomers differ in melting point and solubility. The purity of a mixture is expressed as the enantiomeric excess, ee, which can be obtained from the specific rotation. Cyclohexane adopts a chair conformation, and substituents are more stable in equatorial positions, where they avoid 1,3-diaxial interactions.

substitution-elimination.name: Nucleophilic substitution and elimination
substitution-elimination.description: Check the mechanisms and conditions of SN1, SN2, E1 and E2, the effects of substrate class and solvent, inversion of configuration, carbocation rearrangements, and Zaitsev's and Hofmann's rules with multiple-choice questions.
substitution-elimination.intro:
In reactions of alkyl halides and similar substrates, substitution, in which a nucleophile attacks carbon, competes with elimination, in which a base removes a β-hydrogen. SN2 and E2 proceed in a single step, and their rates depend on both the substrate and the nucleophile (or base). SN1 and E1 are two-step reactions through a carbocation, and their rates depend only on the substrate concentration.
Which reaction dominates depends on the combination of substrate class, the strength and size of the nucleophile, the solvent and the temperature. SN2 goes with inversion of configuration, SN1 tends toward racemization, and carbocations can rearrange. In elimination, Zaitsev's rule, giving the more stable alkene, is the baseline, but with bulky bases the less substituted alkene becomes the major product.

reactions.name: Addition, aromatic and carbonyl reactions
reactions.description: Learn additions to alkenes (Markovnikov's rule, hydroboration), electrophilic aromatic substitution and directing effects, nucleophilic addition to carbonyls, the Grignard reaction, the aldol reaction and reactions of esters with multiple-choice questions.
reactions.intro:
The π bond of an alkene is electron-rich, and electrophiles such as HX and bromine add to it. Addition of HX goes through the more stable carbocation and follows Markovnikov's rule, while hydroboration adds syn with the opposite regiochemistry. A benzene ring undergoes substitution rather than addition, and the substituent already present decides both the orientation, ortho/para or meta, and the rate.
The carbonyl carbon is positively polarized, and nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents, hydrides and enolates add to it. Aldehydes and ketones stop at addition, whereas esters undergo substitution as the leaving group departs. Make sure you understand how equilibrium is handled in esterification and acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, and why saponification is driven to completion by an acid–base reaction.

ir-uv.name: IR, UV-Vis and fluorescence
ir-uv.description: Check characteristic infrared absorptions of functional groups, quantitation with the Beer–Lambert law, conjugation and absorption wavelength, fluorescence and phosphorescence, and quantum yield with multiple-choice and calculation questions.
ir-uv.intro:
Infrared (IR) spectroscopy measures absorption by molecular vibrations and is used to identify functional groups. Typical values are about 1715 cm⁻¹ for C=O, about 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ for hydrogen-bonded O−H and about 2250 cm⁻¹ for C≡N; the vibrational wavenumber is set by bond strength and atomic masses. A vibration that does not change the dipole moment gives no absorption.
Ultraviolet–visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy measures absorption by electronic transitions, and concentrations are found with the Beer–Lambert law, A = εcl. The longer the conjugation, the longer the absorption wavelength. Fluorescence appears at longer wavelengths than absorption and is highly sensitive, but at high concentrations the inner filter effect destroys linearity. Quantum yields are determined by comparison with a reference standard.

nmr-ms.name: NMR and mass spectrometry
nmr-ms.description: Check ¹H NMR chemical shifts, the n+1 rule, integration, equivalent protons and the number of ¹³C NMR signals, along with molecular ions, isotope peaks, the nitrogen rule and fragmentation in mass spectrometry, with multiple-choice questions.
nmr-ms.intro:
In ¹H NMR, the chemical shift δ tells you a proton's environment, the integration tells you how many there are, and splitting by the n+1 rule tells you how many protons sit on the neighboring carbons. Protons near highly electronegative atoms or π electrons appear further downfield. The number of signals in ¹³C NMR reflects the symmetry of the molecule and the number of kinds of equivalent carbons.
In mass spectrometry, the m/z of the molecular ion gives the molecular weight, and isotope peaks, such as Cl (M:M+2 ≈ 3:1) and Br (about 1:1), and the nitrogen rule give clues to composition. Fragments from the McLafferty rearrangement, α-cleavage and so on reveal partial structures, and the accurate mass from high-resolution MS fixes the molecular formula. Combined with IR, these narrow down the structure.

chromatography.name: Chromatography
chromatography.description: Check calculations of retention factor, separation factor, plate number and resolution, the difference between normal phase and reversed phase, GC detectors (FID, TCD, ECD), HPLC gradients and quantitation by the internal standard method with multiple-choice questions.
chromatography.intro:
Chromatography separates components by differences in how they partition between a stationary phase and a mobile phase. The strength of retention is expressed by the retention factor k, the difference in retention between two components by the separation factor α, and column efficiency by the plate number N; the resolution Rs is determined by these three. Because Rs is proportional to √N, changing α is often more effective.
In HPLC, reversed phase, with a nonpolar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase, is the mainstream, and more hydrophobic components elute later. In GC, the detector is chosen for the purpose: the FID, highly sensitive to organic compounds; the universal TCD; and the ECD, highly sensitive to halogenated compounds. For quantitation, the internal standard method, which cancels variations in injection volume, is widely used.

electro-elemental.name: Electroanalytical and elemental analysis
electro-elemental.description: Check the Nernst equation, pH electrodes and calibration, potentiometric titration, voltammetry, atomic absorption and ICP-MS, detection limits and calibration curves, and the basics of significant figures and error with multiple-choice and calculation questions.
electro-elemental.intro:
An electrode potential follows the Nernst equation and is proportional to the logarithm of activity; at 25 °C, for a one-electron reaction, it changes by about 59.2 mV for every tenfold change in activity. pH glass electrodes, ion-selective electrodes and potentiometric titration use this relationship. Voltammetry measures current while sweeping the potential, and combined with preconcentration on the electrode it can measure trace metals.
In elemental analysis, atomic absorption, which measures light absorbed by atoms, ICP optical emission spectrometry, which measures emission in a plasma, and ICP-MS, which measures the masses of ions, are used for different purposes; in ICP-MS, watch out for polyatomic interferences. Whatever the method, calibration curves, detection limits, random and systematic error, and the handling of significant figures are the basis of reliable results.
electro-elemental.blurb: Nernst equation, AAS, ICP, detection limits

volumetric.name: Titrimetric analysis and chemical equilibrium
volumetric.description: Check acid–base titration curves and choosing an indicator, the pH at the equivalence point, complexometric titration with EDTA, precipitation titration and the solubility product, redox titrations with potassium permanganate and iodine, and standardization with primary standards, with multiple-choice and calculation questions.
volumetric.intro:
Titrimetric (volumetric) analysis adds a standard solution of known concentration and finds the amount of analyte from the volume needed to reach the equivalence point, where the reaction is just complete. In acid–base titration, the pH at the equivalence point depends on the strengths of the acid and base: about 7 for a strong acid with a strong base, shifted to the basic side when a weak acid is titrated with a strong base, and to the acidic side when a weak base is titrated with a strong acid. Choose an indicator whose transition range falls within the steep pH change near the equivalence point.
EDTA forms 1:1 complexes with metal ions regardless of their charge and is used to measure water hardness and more. Precipitation titrations are calculated with the solubility product, and redox titrations by the number of electrons exchanged. The concentration of a standard solution is fixed by standardizing it against a pure, stable primary standard, and any error made here carries into every result.

synthesis.name: Strategies in organic synthesis
synthesis.description: Check retrosynthetic analysis, the use of protecting groups, the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling and Heck reaction, the Wittig reaction, the Diels–Alder reaction, choosing oxidizing and reducing agents, and calculating yield and atom economy with multiple-choice questions.
synthesis.intro:
Organic synthesis is planned by retrosynthetic analysis: starting from the target molecule, you disconnect bonds that reliable reactions can form, working backward to readily available starting materials. Functional groups that should not react are temporarily masked with protecting groups and removed after the reaction. Because each protecting group comes off under different conditions, you can handle several functional groups one at a time.
Representative carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions are the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling and the Heck reaction, which join aromatic rings and other fragments with a palladium catalyst; the Wittig reaction, which puts a C=C where a C=O was; and the Diels–Alder reaction, which builds six-membered rings stereospecifically. Choosing oxidizing and reducing agents that stop at the desired stage, and calculating yield based on the limiting reagent, also decide whether a plan is good.

polymer-chem.name: Polymer chemistry
polymer-chem.description: Check addition and condensation polymerization, initiation, propagation and termination in radical polymerization, number-average and weight-average molecular weights and dispersity, the Carothers equation, copolymer composition and molecular-weight measurement by GPC with multiple-choice and calculation questions.
polymer-chem.intro:
Polymers are made by addition polymerization (mostly chain-growth), in which monomers open their C=C double bonds and link one after another, and by condensation polymerization (step-growth), in which functional groups join while releasing water or another small molecule. Radical polymerization proceeds through three stages, initiation, propagation and termination, and high-molecular-weight polymer forms from the very start of the reaction. In condensation polymerization, by contrast, as the Carothers equation Xn = 1/(1 − p) shows, the molecular weight does not rise unless the extent of reaction p is made extremely high.
Because polymer molecular weights have a distribution, you use both the number-average molecular weight Mn, averaged by number, and the weight-average molecular weight Mw, weighted by mass, and express the breadth of the distribution by their ratio Mw/Mn, the dispersity. In the copolymerization of two monomers, the reactivity ratios determine whether the sequence is random, alternating and so on. The molecular-weight distribution is measured by GPC and treated as a value converted by comparison with standards.

thermal-surface.name: Thermal, X-ray and surface analysis
thermal-surface.description: Check the principles and interpretation of TG, DTA and DSC, telling glass transitions from melting, Bragg's law and phase identification by powder XRD, X-ray fluorescence analysis, chemical shifts in XPS, and SEM with EDS, with multiple-choice questions.
thermal-surface.intro:
Thermal analysis measures how a sample's properties change as the temperature is varied. TG gives the amount of dehydration or decomposition from the change in mass, DTA gives the temperatures of endothermic and exothermic events from the temperature difference between the sample and a reference, and DSC gives enthalpies such as the heat of fusion from the difference in heat flow. In DSC, a glass transition appears as a step in the baseline and melting as an endothermic peak, and keep in mind that the shapes change with thermal history.
Among X-ray methods, powder X-ray diffraction identifies crystalline phases from interplanar spacings using Bragg's law, 2d sin θ = λ, and X-ray fluorescence analysis determines composition nondestructively from the characteristic X-rays of each element. XPS probes the elements and their chemical states within a few nm of the surface from chemical shifts, SEM images surface shape and compositional contrast, and EDS analyzes the elements in tiny regions. Use them knowing the different depths from which each obtains information.
